category.name: Operate the Network for Planned Work

derivation: STANDARDS-DERIVED. Every field traces to a standard, a regulation or a recognised industry body per _Collab/SOURCE_AUTHORITY_PACK.md section F, obtained for this category. Nothing is generalised from a client programme or a product.
taxonomy_origin: TAXONOMY ORIGIN, WHICH IS A DIFFERENT FACT FROM THE DERIVATION ABOVE. The derivation line describes where FIELD CONTENT comes from: every field value traces to a standard, a regulation or a recognised industry body and carries its citation. It does NOT describe where the taxonomy comes from. Which processes exist, how they are grouped and what they are called is a practitioner synthesis of delivered implementations, generalised until it is product- and client-neutral. Of the 102 process groups, 43 originate in programme material, 28 in domain research, 20 in a published source and 11 in folder and file names; the provenance layer grades every one and names what to read next. This model is DELIVERED PRACTICE SPECIFIED AGAINST STANDARDS, not a standard turned into a model - and saying so is not a weakness. A taxonomy proven in delivery and then held against the standards is a stronger claim than one derived from a standard and never built.
field_set: EN 17007:2017 cl. 5.2 maintenance process profile, corroborated by ISO 9001:2015 cl. 4.4.1 a) to h).
gaps: This category was written to satisfy nine statements already merged in six other categories - 2.6.3, 3.4.3, 7.3.2, 7.4.1, 9.3.2, 10.2.2, 10.4.2, 10.6.7 and 16.2.3 - which between them reference 18.4.4 twenty-four times and 18.2.2 twelve. All nine hold: 18.4.4 ISSUES the clearance and never consumes one, it does so against a plan approved at 18.2.2, a clearance is not a permit, and emergency isolation at 9.3.2 is a different object.

29 CFR 1910.269(m) specifies the ORDER, which nothing else in this reference does. (m)(2)(i) requires compliance with all of (m)(3) 'in the order specified', so group 18.4 draws a sequence the regulation fixes rather than one the author chose. Where a control cites (m)(3)(vi) it is quoting the rule that the test for voltage comes AFTER the system operator gives the clearance, not describing good practice.

Gas is not a clearance regime and 18.4 branches on commodity for that reason. 1910.269(m) is an electric transmission and distribution rule; a gas isolation runs on 49 CFR 192.605(b)(5), 192.629 purging and 192.751 ignition prevention, with 29 CFR 1910.147 for energy control within its own scope. 18.4.3 has no electric analogue and 18.4.2 has no gas one.

No federal rule sets a planned-outage notice period for electric distribution: 16 U.S.C. 824o keeps distribution outside the bulk-power regime. Notice periods, critical and life-support register criteria, outage priority rules, clearance expiry and abnormal-condition standing instructions are all State, tariff or operator, and all are judgment here.

Only one process is SPEC. 18.4.5 is the live clearance register - a standing record the control room reads continuously, whose issue, transfer and release events are drawn at 18.4.4, 18.4.6 and 18.5.2 where they happen. Everything else in the category has an instance.

Both public frameworks reach this category, unlike 11.0: GFMAM subject 3.8 Shutdown and Outage Strategy and Planning and APQC PCF Utilities 14.1.6 Perform planned network operation (19285) both name it.

Boundaries held deliberately: 3.4.3 consumes the WINDOW from 18.2.2 and 18.2.3 and never the clearance; 9.0 owns emergency isolation and switching during restoration; 19.1.3 coordinates energisation of NEW assets while 18.5.3 returns existing plant to service; 12.1 holds the asset register while 18.5.5 holds the operating state; 13.1.2 holds the material reservation that 18.2.5 tests.

49 CFR 192.605(a) requires abnormal-operations procedures for TRANSMISSION lines only. A distribution operator is not obliged to hold them, which is why 18.1.5 is a case built on operator practice rather than on the rule.

processes.name: Determine the isolation the work requires
processes.intent: Decide what has to be isolated for the work, and which energy-control regime applies.
activities: Take the work, its location and what it will touch
Determine the extent of isolation the work needs
Determine the regime: 1910.269(m), 1910.147 or gas operating
Return the isolation extent and the regime that governs it

trigger.text: Work has been scheduled that cannot proceed on a live network.

inputs.what: Commodity and voltage or pressure class

controls.text: 29 CFR 1910.269(m)(1) is explicit: anything deenergized under procedures other than (d) or (m) SHALL BE TREATED AS ENERGIZED. Choosing the wrong regime does not produce a weaker protection, it produces none.
(m)(2) turns on whether a system operator is in charge of the lines and their means of disconnection. That decides who holds the clearance and is settled here, not in the field.
Gas is not a clearance. 49 CFR 192.605(b)(5) start-up and shutdown within MAOP is the operating discipline; 29 CFR 1910.147 covers energy control within its own scope.

notation.why: The output is an isolation extent and the regime that governs it - values, and the regime tests are stated in the rule rather than inferred.

processes.name: Create the switching or diversion plan
processes.intent: Write the switching or diversion plan that will produce the isolation.
activities: Take the required isolation extent
Identify every point through which energy could be supplied
Sequence the operations, including remote and automatic controls
Record the plan and the state it will leave the network in

trigger.text: An isolation extent and regime have been determined.

outputs.what: Abnormal state the plan will create

controls.text: 29 CFR 1910.269(m)(3)(ii) requires EVERY switch, disconnector, jumper and tap through which a known source could supply the section to be open. Opening the obvious ones is not a plan.

(m)(3)(iii) requires automatically and remotely controlled switches that could reclose the opened means to be tagged at the point of control and the control feature disabled. Remote reclose is the failure mode this addresses.
A diversion that keeps customers on supply is still an isolation plan and takes the same discipline. 9.0 switches during restoration; this is planned work only.

processes.intent: Establish who loses supply, for how long, and who has to be told.
activities: Trace the customers and third parties on the affected section

inputs.what: Customers and premises on the section

controls.text: Third parties attached to the structures are affected parties too. 11.4.1 holds who they are and 18.3.1 will notify them; an impact list that counts only metered customers understates the outage.
No source in the pack sets an outage-duration estimating method or a customer-minutes threshold. Both are the operator's.

processes.name: Verify the plan against the current network state
processes.intent: Check the plan against the network as it actually stands today.
activities: Compare the plan's assumed states to the current device states
Test each device the plan operates for known defects
Identify abnormal conditions already in force
Return the plan verified, or send it back with what changed

trigger.text: A switching plan is ready for verification before approval.

inputs.what: Defect and maintenance history on the devices

outputs.what: Plan returned with the discrepancy named

controls.text: 49 CFR 192.747 requires a valve necessary for safe operation to be checked and serviced at intervals not exceeding 15 months, at least once each calendar year, and an inoperable valve to get prompt remedial action unless an alternative is designated. Isolating on an overdue valve is not verified.
A plan written against last week's network state is a plan against a network that no longer exists. 18.5.5 keeps the as-operated record true and this process depends on it.
Abnormal conditions already in force change what the plan will actually achieve, and 18.1.5 holds them.

measures.name: Verification catch rate
measures.definition: Share of plans returned at verification rather than failing at execution.
measures.cite: SMRP Best Practices, Pillar 5 Work Management 5.4.1 Rework

variants: Plan verified against a current network model
Plan returned because a device state changed
Plan returned because a valve or switch is defective
Plan revised for an abnormal condition already in force

processes.name: Determine abnormal-condition and contingency arrangements
processes.intent: Decide what happens if the network cannot be returned as planned.
activities: Identify what the isolation leaves without redundancy
Agree the abnormal conditions that will stand during the work
Agree the contingency if the work overruns or fails
Record the standing instruction the control room will operate to

trigger.text: A verified plan leaves the network in a reduced or abnormal state.

controls.text: Two competent operators will trade redundancy, weather risk and the cost of aborting in a different order, and the right answer depends on which of them is binding on the day. That is why this is a case.
The abort arrangement has to be agreed BEFORE the clearance is issued. Deciding how to abandon an isolation while standing in it is not a decision, it is a reaction.
An abnormal condition that persists past the work is a network state, not an outage note. 18.5.5 records it and 18.1.4 will read it back on the next plan.

Reduced redundancy with a standing instruction for the duration
Weather-dependent abort arrangement
Abnormal condition intended to persist beyond the work

notation.why: Redundancy, weather and abort cost are all live and two operators will not settle them in the same order.

group.name: Approve and schedule planned network operations

processes.intent: Put the outage plan in front of the authority that can approve it.
activities: Assemble the plan, impact and contingency into one submission
Route it to the approving authority for the network involved
Attach the work the outage exists to enable
Track it against the notice the outage will need

trigger.text: A verified plan with its impact and contingency is ready to submit.

outputs.what: Submission lead time against the notice required

controls.text: A submission that arrives inside the customer notice period forces a choice between an unnotified outage and a deferred one. The lead time is checked here rather than discovered at 18.3.
The outage exists to enable work. A request that does not carry the work it enables cannot be prioritised against a competing one at 18.2.4.

Where the network is bulk-power rather than local distribution, 16 U.S.C. 824o brings a different coordination regime; this reference covers distribution and says so rather than implying the transmission process.

processes.name: Approve, reject or defer the outage plan

group.name: Approve and schedule planned network operations

processes.intent: Approve, reject or defer the outage plan, and say on what basis.
activities: Test the plan, its impact and its contingency against the network state
Test it against competing demands on the same network
Return approve, approve-with-conditions, defer or reject
Record the basis and any condition the approval carries

trigger.text: A submitted outage request needs a decision before it can be scheduled.

inputs.what: Competing requests on the same network

outputs.what: Approved, conditioned, deferred or rejected plan

controls.text: This approval is what 29 CFR 1910.269(m)(3)(i) later rests on: the employee in charge requests deenergization of a particular section, and the section is the one this approval fixed. An approval that does not name the section is not an approval.
Twelve references in six merged categories treat 18.2.2 as the producer of an APPROVED SWITCHING PLAN. It must therefore output an object, not a state on somebody else's record.
Defer is a real outcome and is not a soft reject. A deferred plan keeps its verification; a rejected one returns to 18.1.2.

measures.definition: Distribution of approve, condition, defer and reject over the period.

Rejected back to planning

processes.name: Schedule the planned network operation

group.name: Approve and schedule planned network operations

processes.intent: Put the approved operation in the calendar, with the work it enables.
activities: Take the approved plan and its conditions
Fix the window and the crews for the switching itself
Bind the work that will run inside the window
Publish the window to notice and to the work schedule

trigger.text: An outage plan has been approved and needs a window.

inputs.what: The work to run inside the window

outputs.what: Scheduled network operation with a window
Window published to notice and to 3.4

controls.text: 3.4.3 consumes the WINDOW from this process and from 18.2.2 - not the clearance. The window is a schedule object; the clearance is a safety object issued on the day at 18.4.4. Merging them is the most common error in this whole area.
The switching itself needs crews and they are scheduled here. An outage window with no switching resource is a window nobody can open.
3.4 places the work inside the window. This process does not become a second scheduler for that work.

processes.name: Resolve conflicting or competing outage requests

group.name: Approve and schedule planned network operations

processes.intent: Settle which outage happens when two want the same network at the same time.
activities: Identify the requests that cannot coexist
Establish what each is enabling and what deferring it costs
Negotiate a combined window, a sequence or a deferral
Record the decision and tell the losing request why

trigger.text: Two or more approved or submitted outages contend for the same network.

controls.text: Combining two outages into one window beats sequencing them and beats taking the network out twice, but both plans need re-verifying at 18.1.4 against the combined state.

No source states an outage priority rule. What a deferral costs - a compliance date, a customer commitment, a crew already mobilised - is the operator's to weigh and two schedulers weigh it differently.
A deferred request that is not told why comes back unchanged next week and contends again.

controls.text: An outage taken for work that turns out to have no material is the most expensive failure in this category: the network is out, the customers are off and nothing is achieved. 13.1.2 holds the reservation and this is where it is tested.
Returning the window early is cheap. Discovering it on the day costs the outage, the crews and the customer minutes.
Where a contractor will do the work, the 29 CFR 1910.269(a)(3) host and contract employer information exchange is owed before the crew arrives, and 16.2.3 is where it happens.

10.1.4 holds the contact and notification preference. This process resolves the list; it does not keep a second copy of the preferences.
A party with no reachable channel is a finding, not an omission. It goes on the exception list so 18.3.2 can escalate rather than silently skip it.

Test the lines and equipment with a device designed to detect voltage

Only then treat the section as deenergized

controls.text: 49 CFR 192.629: purge air with gas, or gas with air, in a MODERATELY RAPID AND CONTINUOUS FLOW; where that cannot prevent a hazardous mixture, a SLUG OF INERT GAS goes in first.

49 CFR 192.751(a): where a hazardous amount of gas is vented into open air, every potential ignition source is removed and a fire extinguisher is provided. (b) forbids welding or cutting on pipe containing a combustible mixture and (c) requires warning signs where appropriate.
This process has no electric analogue. An electric section is proved dead by testing at 18.4.2; a gas section is made safe by purging, and the two are not interchangeable steps.

controls.text: 29 CFR 1910.269(m)(3)(xii): no-one may remove tags without release of the associated clearance. The register is what makes the association knowable, and a tag whose clearance nobody can find is a tag nobody can lawfully remove.
(m)(3)(xiii) forbids reenergizing until ALL crews working the lines release THEIR clearances. A register that shows one clearance where two exist will reenergize onto a crew.

Work stopped is as valid a trigger as work complete. A clearance held open over an abandoned job blocks the network and the crew who could have used the window.

Reverse the switching to the normal configuration

trigger.text: The last clearance on a section has been cancelled.

controls.text: 29 CFR 1910.269(m)(3)(xiii) is a four-part bar on reenergizing: no-one initiates it until ALL protective grounds are removed, ALL crews working the lines release THEIR clearances, ALL employees are clear, and ALL protective tags are removed from that point of disconnection.
The automatic and remote controls disabled at 18.4.1 under (m)(3)(iii) are re-enabled here. A section restored with its reclosing blocked is not restored; the next fault finds out.
Gas returns to service under 49 CFR 192.605(b)(5) within MAOP plus the allowed build-up, and a purge back to gas runs under 192.629. Neither is a clearance release.

controls.text: 18.1.4 verifies the next plan against this record. An as-operated state that is a day out of date turns plan verification into a formality and puts the error back into the field.
An abnormal condition left standing is part of the network state, not a note on a closed job. Recording it here is what makes 18.1.5 able to read it back.
